## Simple explanation

A large language model, or LLM, is a neural network trained on large amounts of
text so it can process and generate language. It can answer questions, draft
text, summarize documents, and perform other language tasks when given an
instruction or context.

## Technical explanation

Most modern LLMs are based on the Transformer architecture. During
pretraining, the model learns statistical patterns in token sequences, often
by predicting a next token. The result is a parameterized model that maps an
input context to a probability distribution over possible next tokens.

The word "large" is relative and may refer to model parameters, training data,
compute, or a combination of them. Size alone does not determine quality:
training data, architecture, post-training, inference setup, and evaluation
all matter.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

LLMs power conversational interfaces, code assistants, retrieval-augmented
systems, and many agent workflows. Engineers must account for context limits,
latency, inference cost, reliability, safety, and the difference between
generated text and verified facts.

## How it works

Text is divided into tokens and converted to numerical representations. A
Transformer processes the token sequence, using attention to relate tokens to
one another. At generation time, the model repeatedly selects or samples a
next token and appends it to the context.

The model's output is not a database lookup: it is generated from learned
parameters and the current context. External tools or retrieval systems can
provide additional information when needed.

## Practical example

A support assistant can receive a user's question together with relevant
product documentation, then generate a response grounded in that material.
The LLM handles language generation; retrieval and application logic help
provide the right evidence and enforce product rules.

## Common misconceptions

- An LLM does not reliably know whether every generated statement is true.
- A larger parameter count does not guarantee better performance for every task.
- Prompting alone is not the same as training or fine-tuning a model.
- LLM and chatbot are not synonyms: a chatbot is an application that may use an LLM.
